\section[\gu{નમસ્તે}]{\gu{નમસ્તે} (namaste) — \textquotedblleft{}hello,\textquotedblright{} and a script with no ceiling}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-namaste}



\begin{quote}
The first Gujarati word — and your first look at a script that is Devanagari's sister, but bareheaded.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\emph{(If you already read Gujarati, skim this.)} Gujarati runs \textbf{left to right}, and every consonant carries a built-in \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}: \textbf{\gu{ન}} na, \textbf{\gu{મ}} ma, \textbf{\gu{સ}} sa, \textbf{\gu{ત}} ta. A \emph{virama} strips the vowel so it joins the next as a conjunct: \textbf{\gu{સ} + \gu{્} + \gu{ત} $\to$ \gu{સ્ત}}. And the one thing to notice above all: Gujarati has \textbf{no top line}. Hindi, Marathi, and Bengali hang their letters from a horizontal bar (the \emph{shirorekhā}); Gujarati cut that bar away, so its letters float free. It is sometimes called \textquotedblleft{}the headless script\textquotedblright{} — the quickest way to tell it from Devanagari at a glance.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{નમસ્તે}} (\emph{namaste}) is Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{નમસ્}} (\emph{namas}, \textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\gu{તે}} (\emph{te}, \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I bow to you},\textquotedblright{} the very same word as in Hindi and Sanskrit. Gujarati is \textbf{Indo-Aryan}, a granddaughter of Sanskrit, so it inherited this greeting whole. (An even more common Gujarati hello, among Hindus, is \textbf{\gu{કેમ} \gu{છો}?} \emph{kem chho?} — \textquotedblleft{}how are you?\textquotedblright{} — which you will build in Chapter 3.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}namaste\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one visible difference from Devanagari (no top line)
  \item its two parts (\emph{namas} \textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{te} \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{namaste} mean, and what marks Gujarati apart from Devanagari at a glance? (\textquotedblleft{}I bow to you\textquotedblright{}; it has no top line — the \textquotedblleft{}headless\textquotedblright{} script.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{આભાર}]{\gu{આભાર} (ābhār) — \textquotedblleft{}thank you,\textquotedblright{} an obligation gladly owed}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-aabhaar}



\begin{quote}
Gujarati's everyday \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} — and it comes from the idea of being \emph{indebted}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} (the independent long \emph{ā}, for a word-initial vowel) + \textbf{\gu{ભા}} (\emph{bhā}) + \textbf{\gu{ર}} (\emph{r}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhār}). Note again: no top line.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhār}, \textquotedblleft{}thanks, gratitude\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{આભાર}} (\emph{ābhāra}, \textquotedblleft{}a burden, an obligation\textquotedblright{}), from \textbf{\gu{આ}-} (\emph{ā-}, \textquotedblleft{}toward\textquotedblright{}) + the root \textbf{\gu{ભૃ}} (\emph{bhṛ}, \textquotedblleft{}to bear, carry\textquotedblright{}). To thank someone is to acknowledge you now \emph{bear an obligation} to them — the same idea as English \textbf{oblige} (Latin \emph{ob-} + \emph{ligāre} \textquotedblleft{}to bind\textquotedblright{}) and Portuguese \emph{obrigado}. That root \emph{bhṛ} is Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, the ancestor of English \textbf{bear} (to carry) and Latin \emph{ferre}. (The more Sanskritic \textbf{\gu{ધન્યવાદ}} \emph{dhanyavād} is also used, but \emph{ābhār} is the warm, everyday Gujarati word.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ābhār\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally acknowledges (an obligation \textquotedblleft{}borne\textquotedblright{})
  \item the English cousin of its root \emph{bhṛ} (\textbf{bear}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{ābhār} literally mean, and what English word shares its root? (\textquotedblleft{}An obligation borne\textquotedblright{}; \textbf{bear} — from PIE \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{આવજો}]{\gu{આવજો} (āvjo) — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{} (come again)}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-aavjo}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Gujarati goodbye — and, like the goodbyes across all of India, it is really an invitation to return.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} (independent \emph{ā}) + \textbf{\gu{વ}} (\emph{va}) + \textbf{\gu{જો}} (\emph{jo}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{આવજો}} (\emph{āvjo}) is the polite imperative of \textbf{\gu{આવવું}} (\emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}please{]} come {[}again{]}}.\textquotedblright{} A Gujarati never signs off by saying \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving\textquotedblright{}; the parting word is \emph{come}. It is the same \textquotedblleft{}promise of return\textquotedblright{} that runs through the whole subcontinent — Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}), Bengali \emph{āshi} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come\textquotedblright{}), Hindi \emph{phir milenge} (\textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}) — here made into a single warm word built on the verb \emph{to come}. (To one person, familiarly: \textbf{\gu{આવજે}} \emph{āvje}.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}āvjo\textquotedblright{}
  \item what it literally means (\textquotedblleft{}{[}please{]} come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{})
  \item the verb it's built on (\emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Gujarati goodbye literally say, and what verb is it from? (\textquotedblleft{}Come {[}again{]}\textquotedblright{}; \emph{āvvũ}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{} — never \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{હા} / \gu{ના}]{\gu{હા} / \gu{ના} (hā / nā) — \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-haa-naa}



\begin{quote}
Two tiny words no conversation survives without — and one is a cousin of English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{હા}} (\emph{hā}) = \textbf{\gu{હ}} (\emph{ha}) + the long-\emph{ā} sign. \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}) = \textbf{\gu{ન}} (\emph{na}) + the long-\emph{ā} sign.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{હા}} (\emph{hā}, \textquotedblleft{}yes\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\gu{ના}} (\emph{nā}, \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}). The \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} rides the ancient negative \textbf{na-} — the very same Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*ne} behind English \textbf{no}, \textbf{not}, \textbf{none}, Latin \emph{nōn}, Hindi \emph{nahīṁ}, and Bengali \emph{nā}. Of all the words in this book, this \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} reaches furthest unchanged: one syllable spoken, in some form, from Iceland to Gujarat for five thousand years.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hā\textquotedblright{} (yes) and \textquotedblleft{}nā\textquotedblright{} (no)
  \item the shared ancestor of \emph{nā} and English \emph{no} (PIE \emph{*ne})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ancient root links Gujarati \emph{nā} to English \emph{no}? (Proto-Indo- European \emph{*ne}, \textquotedblleft{}not.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[\gu{સારું}]{\gu{સારું} (sārũ) — \textquotedblleft{}good,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}okay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-saarun}



\begin{quote}
The all-purpose \textquotedblleft{}good / fine / okay / alright\textquotedblright{} — and your first taste of Gujarati's three genders.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{સા}} (\emph{sā}) + \textbf{\gu{રું}} (\emph{rũ}, with the nasal \emph{anusvāra} on the \emph{u}) $\to$ \textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}, \textquotedblleft{}good, fine, okay\textquotedblright{}) is from Sanskrit \textbf{\gu{સાર}} (\emph{sāra}, \textquotedblleft{}essence, substance, the best part\textquotedblright{}) — the same \emph{sāra} behind Bengali's \emph{sāramilla} (\textquotedblleft{}no matter\textquotedblright{}). As \textquotedblleft{}okay/agreed\textquotedblright{} it oils every Gujarati conversation, the way English uses \textquotedblleft{}alright.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: three genders, on the adjective}]
Look at that ending \textbf{-\gu{ું}} (\emph{-ũ}). Gujarati, like Marathi, keeps \textbf{three} genders from Sanskrit — masculine, feminine, \textbf{and neuter} — where Hindi and Punjabi kept only two. An adjective agrees with its noun in all three:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારો}} (\emph{sāro}) — masculine
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારી}} (\emph{sārī}) — feminine
  \item \textbf{\gu{સારું}} (\emph{sārũ}) — \textbf{neuter}
\end{itemize}

Standing alone as \textquotedblleft{}okay,\textquotedblright{} it takes the neuter \emph{sārũ}. You will meet this three-way agreement on every adjective and possessive.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}sārũ\textquotedblright{} — good / okay
  \item the three genders — \emph{sāro} (m.) / \emph{sārī} (f.) / \emph{sārũ} (n.)
  \item the Sanskrit root (\emph{sāra}, \textquotedblleft{}essence\textquotedblright{})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{sārũ} mean, and what does its \emph{-ũ} ending tell you? (\textquotedblleft{}Good / okay\textquotedblright{}; it is the \textbf{neuter} — Gujarati keeps three genders.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 1 — The greetings}

\label{lesson:GU-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The five greetings, mixed and recombined.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{How to answer — rapid recall}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item hello / goodbye — \emph{namaste}
  \item thank you — \emph{ābhār}
  \item yes and no — \emph{hā} / \emph{nā}
  \item good / okay — \emph{sārũ}
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}come again\textquotedblright{} goodbye — \emph{āvjo}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Script — the script and the language}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the one visible thing that sets Gujarati apart from Devanagari (no top line)
  \item how many genders Gujarati keeps (three — \emph{sāro/sārī/sārũ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — roots you now carry}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{namaste} = \emph{namas} \textquotedblleft{}a bow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{te} \textquotedblleft{}to you\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{ābhār} $\leftarrow$ \emph{ā} + \emph{bhṛ} \textquotedblleft{}to bear\textquotedblright{} $\to$ an obligation borne (cousin of English \emph{bear})
  \item \emph{nā} (\textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{}) $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*ne} $\to$ English \emph{no/not/none}
  \item \emph{āvjo} (\textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}come {[}again{]},\textquotedblright{} from \emph{āvvũ} \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Someone thanks you and turns to leave. Answer their thanks and send them off the Gujarati way. (\emph{Sārũ} — and \emph{āvjo}, \textquotedblleft{}come again.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
